Poland and Lithuania were joined by a royal marriage in 1385 and merged into a single Commonwealth in 1569. At its height in the early 1600s it was one of the largest and most populous states in Europe, stretching from the Baltic almost to the Black Sea, until its neighbours divided it out of existence between 1772 and 1795.

The union began when the pagan Grand Duke of Lithuania, Jogaila, married the young Polish queen Jadwiga, became a Catholic and took the Polish crown; Lithuania was baptised soon after. The joint army crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410. The Union of Lublin in 1569 made the two a single state with a shared king and parliament.

What made it unusual:

  • The nobility, the szlachta, was large, perhaps a tenth of the people, and it ruled.
  • From 1573 the king was elected by the nobles, and each new king had to swear to their rights.
  • The Sejm, the parliament, came to need every vote: a single member could block it with the liberum veto.
  • The Warsaw Confederation of 1573 promised peace among faiths, at a time when much of Europe was at war over religion.

Grain exports down the Vistula to Amsterdam made the landowners rich and bound the peasants as serfs. In 1683 King John III Sobieski led the relief army at the Battle of Vienna, which broke the Ottoman siege of the city.

The 1600s brought wars with Sweden, Russia and Cossack rebels, and the state weakened. Russia, Prussia and Austria took it apart in the three Partitions of Poland. A reform constitution of 3 May 1791, one of the first written constitutions in Europe, came too late. Poland only returned as a state in 1918.
